articles.title: Thailand Launches Mandatory ISSB-Aligned Sustainability Reporting for Public Companies - ESG Today
articles.summary: Thailand Launches Mandatory ISSB-Aligned Sustainability Reporting for Public Companies  ESG Today
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced the publication of new regulations requiring listed companies to provide sustainability and climate-related reporting aligned with the IFRS Foundation’s International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) standards.
Reporting requirements under the new regulation will begin in 2028, covering the 2027 year, for the largest companies, and be phased in through 2031 for other listed companies and investment entities.
The new regulation marks a significant shift towards enabling standardized sustainability reporting for public companies. The SEC has required listed companies to disclose information on ESG performance, governance, human rights, and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions as part of their annual reporting since 2022, but did not rely on a single standard, instead allowing companies to utilize external frameworks, such as the Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Standards or TCFD recommendations.
In 2024, the SEC launched a consultation to explore shifting sustainability reporting to the IFRS standards, to improve international alignment and enable more consistent and comparable data.
The ISSB released its inaugural general sustainability and climate reporting standards, IFRS S1 and IFRS S2, respectively, in June 2023. To date, more than 45 jurisdictions have started the process to use the standards.
Under the new regulations, constituents of SET50, the 50 largest companies on the Stock Exchange of Thailand will begin ISSB-aligned reporting in 2028 (on 2027 data), followed by SET100 companies in 2029, all other SET-listed in 2030, and all listed companies on the secondary mai exchange as well as REITs, IFFs, IFTs, and PFs.
The regulations also include a requirement for GHG emissions disclosure to be verified by assurance providers in accordance with internationally accepted assurance standards.
The new regulations include a series of transition reliefs to support companies’ development of data systems and capabilities, including exemption from comparative information in the first year of reporting the disclosure of climate-related information, flexibility in the reporting timeframe, use of equivalent GHG emissions, calculation standards and exemption from disclosure of Scope 3 GHG emissions during the initial period of implementation.

articles.summary: British sport under-prepared for climate risks as costs rise, report says  The Straits Times

LONDON, Nov 5 - Climate change is becoming a growing threat to British sport, damaging facilities, disrupting fixtures, increasing costs and deterring participation, according to a report that warns the sector is dangerously under-prepared for extreme weather.
Every organisation surveyed reported being affected by extreme weather in 2026 and 94% said sport was under-prepared for climate change. Yet a separate review of professional club disclosures found only nine had explicitly identified climate or extreme weather as a business risk.
The report by the British Association for Sustainable Sport (BASIS) paints a stark picture of a sporting landscape built for weather conditions that no longer exist, with impacts felt from Premier League stadiums to grassroots playing fields.
"Sport is already paying the price for climate change through damaged grounds, rising insurance costs, lost match-day income and lost opportunities for people to be active," BASIS founder Russell Seymour said in the report.
"The game has changed. Extreme weather is no longer a series of isolated disruptions; it is a material, recurring and intensifying business risk."
Among more than 200 clubs, venues and governing bodies surveyed, 86% reported being affected by extreme heat, 78% by drought, 31% by storm damage and 28% by flooding.
The financial risks are becoming increasingly apparent.

"If a club with Manchester United's scale and resources considers this risk sufficiently material to disclose to investors, smaller and less financially resilient institutions cannot reasonably treat it as peripheral," the report said.
Worcestershire County Cricket Club's flood-prone New Road ground has repeatedly faced questions about its long-term viability, and Carlisle United have described flood insurance for Brunton Park as increasingly unaffordable.
The report also highlighted the effect on competition schedules. Research cited by BASIS found at least 118 weather-related postponements across the top six tiers of English men's football between the 2021-22 and 2025-26 seasons, with lower-league and non-league clubs bearing the brunt.
Cancelled or rearranged matches can mean lower attendances and reduced revenue for lower division clubs operating on tight budgets.

The AI Power Boom: Investing Through Carbon Markets
How growing electricity demand is creating a new investment driver across global compliance carbon markets
AI is driving one of the largest increases in electricity demand in decades. The International Energy Agency (IEA) projects global data center electricity consumption will nearly double, from 485 terawatt-hours (TWh) in 2025 to 950 TWh in 2030, with AI-focused demand roughly tripling.1 As data centers multiply, power is becoming one of the defining economic consequences of AI adoption.
Capturing that growth through a differentiated exposure is not straightforward. Many of the most compelling AI names remain private, while publicly traded companies often carry high valuations and are already heavily represented in broad equity portfolios. Meanwhile, electricity is difficult to invest in directly, and energy commodities carry storage and seasonality costs, meaning a compelling long-term electricity-demand thesis does not necessarily translate into a practical investment.
Compliance carbon allowances offer an alternative way to access this trend by targeting another measurable consequence of AI’s power demand: emissions from electricity generation. At the current pace of growth, AI data centers in the US could emit as much carbon dioxide each year as 5 to 10 million passenger cars through the end of this decade.2 In regions that regulate emissions under cap-and-invest programs — including the EU, California, participating Eastern US states, and Washington state — incremental electricity demand that is met by additional fossil-fuel generation could drive an increase in compliance demand for carbon allowances.
How AI’s Power Demand Reinforces Carbon’s Supply-Driven Investment Case
The investment case rests on two powerful forces converging: policy-driven reductions in allowance supply, as governments progressively tighten emissions caps, and a potential new source of compliance demand from AI's growing power needs. We believe this combination gives investors something AI equities cannot. It offers exposure to the AI build-out without identifying the winning model developer, chipmaker, hyperscaler, or data center operator, alongside a second, independent driver in legislated supply reductions. And where new demand meets a market whose surplus is already shrinking, even modest additions may tighten balances meaningfully.
Figure 1: How AI-driven electricity demand can increase compliance carbon allowance demand
Virginia: A Real-World Case Study
Virginia provides a tangible example of how the AI power boom can intersect with compliance carbon markets. Home to one of the world’s largest concentrations of data centers, the state faces rapidly growing electricity requirements just as its power sector has re-entered the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative (RGGI). The program requires covered fossil-fuel power generators with 25 megawatts (MW) or more capacity across participating Eastern US states to surrender allowances against their emissions.
The scale of Virginia's data center industry makes this connection particularly relevant. Data centers accounted for approximately 28% of Dominion Energy Virginia’s electricity sales in 2025,3 with roughly 700 facilities operating or in the pipeline concentrated in Northern Virginia’s “Data Center Alley."4 The state's lead reflects its fiber and subsea cable infrastructure, historically competitive power prices, tax incentives, and proximity to federal agencies.
Expectations surrounding Virginia's return to RGGI contributed to a sharp repricing, as participants weighed the state's substantial power-sector emissions and growing electricity needs against tightening market supply. Following the official April 24 announcement on Virginia's re-entry into the program, RGGI allowance prices nearly doubled from the start of the year, reaching a record high of approximately $52 in early May. Although prices have eased from their peak, RGGI allowances remain up 51% year-to-date as of October 26, 2026, trading around $40 per short ton.5
Figure 2: RGGI allowance price performance following Virginia's re-entry announcement
Beyond the initial repricing, the longer-term question is how Virginia’s additional electricity demand will be met. Resources for the Future’s (RFF) June 2026 analysis assumes in-state natural-gas generation supplies 80% of overall load growth, with the remainder from zero-carbon or non-RGGI sources.6Applying that assumption, along with two lower illustrative scenarios, a hypothetical 20 TWh increase in data center demand would require roughly 2.6 million to 7.1 million additional RGGI allowances a year.7
Figure 3: Illustrative additional annual RGGI allowance demand under data center load-growth scenarios
The supply outlook puts these figures into perspective. From 2027, RGGI’s new cap trajectory declines by about 11 million short tons a year through 2033, nearly four times the previous rate.8 Together with Virginia's return, this is projected to reduce RGGI’s bank of surplus allowances to about 20 million short tons by the end of 2030, from 35 million previously.9 While the expanded reserve may provide some near-term supply flexibility, the steeper cap could become a more significant price driver as the allowance surplus declines. This matters because the price impact of new demand depends on how much of a supply buffer the market has. Where a large surplus exists, incremental emissions can be absorbed. Where it is nearly exhausted, and caps are falling, even modest increases in demand may have an outsized effect on prices.
Virginia illustrates how accelerating electricity demand can create additional compliance demand for carbon allowances at a time when regulatory policy is constraining supply.
Beyond Virginia: A Broader Opportunity Across Global Carbon Markets
The opportunity extends beyond RGGI to California and the EU, where rising electricity demand also meets tightening allowance supply. Differences in generation mix and regulation create distinct market effects, diversifying exposure across established carbon programs rather than concentrating it in one region.
Powering Data Centers with Existing Gas Infrastructure: California Spotlight
California's Cap-and-Invest program offers another important expression of the same theme. Data centers accounted for about 1,000 MW, or 2% of California Independent System Operator (CAISO)'s peak electricity demand, in early 2026, a figure projected to rise to 4,500 MW, or 9%, by 2040.10 Unlike RGGI, California’s program extends beyond in-state power generation to cover emissions associated with imported electricity, alongside fuel distributors and large industrial facilities. As data center demand grows, any incremental emissions from covered in-state generation or electricity imports could add to compliance demand for California Carbon Allowances (CCAs).
The proposed 275 MW Golden Valley Technology Hub in Kern County illustrates one potential pathway: developed by Beacon Data Centers and California Resources Corporation, the campus would draw power from the existing compliance-regulated 550 MW Elk Hills gas plant. To the extent that serving the campus requires additional gas generation, the resulting emissions could increase demand for CCAs.
This potential demand-side growth comes as supply tightens sharply. Reforms adopted in May 2026 cut allowance budgets by 11% a year from 2027 to 2030, up from about 4%, helping push the market into cumulative deficit by 2033.11 CCA prices are currently trading at $32 as of October 26, 2026, just $2 above the projected 2027 auction reserve price.12 The reserve price sets a minimum price at government auctions and increases annually by 5% plus inflation, providing a rising downside benchmark for the market.
Europe's Rising Power Demand Meets Grid Constraints
Europe provides a further example. Data center electricity consumption across the EU is projected to rise 68%, from 68 TWh in 2024 to 114 TWh by 2030,13 as the EU targets a tripling of data center capacity within the next five to seven years.14 This material increase in energy demand adds pressure to electricity systems already navigating renewable-energy deployment, transmission constraints, and the retirement of conventional generation. Additional demand may require continued gas-fired generation where renewable output and grid capacity fall short.
For the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS), the key investment implication may be less about an increase in absolute emissions and more about a slower pace of decarbonization. This dynamic was evident in the first half of 2026, when EU power-sector emissions rose 2% year-on-year despite record wind and solar output, as gas generation increased.15 While the increase was not attributed specifically to data centers, it illustrates continued reliance on fossil generation when clean supply falls short. Additional AI-related demand could similarly slow the decline in covered power-sector emissions, sustaining demand for EU Allowances (EUAs) as the cap continues to tighten, falling 4.3% a year through 2027 and 4.4% a year from 2028.16
Overall, the scale and structure of each market differ, but the mechanism is the same: growing electricity demand meets a tightening allowance supply.

Digger: A climate warning in a very expensive suit—and 5 ways to strengthen sustainability
Contains plot spoilers: this movie reveals an exaggerated future that reminds us why humanity needs sustainable business.
Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger is a climate-disaster satire disguised as a power fantasy for outsize corporations. Tom Cruise plays Digger Rockwell, a third-generation oil magnate whose Greenland drilling operation triggers a methane disaster and sends a massive ice shelf drifting toward Europe. When scientists warn that the consequences could be catastrophic, Digger’s response becomes a study of what happens when urgency, uncertainty and competing priorities collide.
The premise is deliberately absurd, and that is part of its power. The film exaggerates climate denial, corporate greenwashing, and political deference until they become almost operatic. Digger believes that wealth, influence and force of personality can outweigh evidence and the natural world’s limits.
Dr. Nirav Ganesh, played by Riz Ahmed, is Digger’s environmental safety chief and scientific adviser. He understands what is happening, can clarify the consequences, and keeps trying to ensure decision-makers understand the risks of inaction. In a cast of caricatures, Ganesh is the voice of scientific clarity, which also makes him the person delivering the hardest news.
Anyone who has worked alongside sustainability professionals will recognize Ganesh. They often ask the questions that slow a conversation down but improve the decision: What is the impact? Who is affected? What evidence supports this claim? What happens if the plan does not work? What are we missing?
Their job is not to disrupt progress or make companies appear less ambitious. At least not intentionally. Sustainability leaders exist to help organizations become more credible, resilient and responsible.
The problem isn’t the difficult questions corporations must answer. It is the increased risk exposure from setting those questions aside when they feel inconvenient, unfamiliar, or expensive. In Digger, the warning is imminent and disturbing. The tragedy occurs when those with the authority to respond do not enable the conditions to hear it.
Sustainability is back, though it never really left
Sustainability is swinging back into public dialogue, but the conversation is becoming more practical and less comfortable. Organizations are being asked to explain their environmental commitments and how those commitments affect social risks, including jobs, communities, customers, investors, technology and long-term competitiveness.
Sustainability should not be treated as a communications accessory or a collection of buzzwords. Nor should it require companies to portray themselves as villains for operating in complex industries. Large organizations create jobs, develop infrastructure, support communities and have the resources to help build a more resilient economy. Digger reminds us to consider how companies can use their position and influence thoughtfully. The film foreshadows what can happen when we treat Mother Nature as a competitor, dismiss expert advice because it’s inconvenient, and assume communications can contain operational reality.
The film’s United Nations parody scenes push a man-made climate catastrophe to a farcical extreme. But the underlying point is something to think about: if business, governments, regulators, scientists and civil society operate in separate silos, a shared crisis can become a blame-filled brawl rather than a coordinated response.
With COP31 fast approaching in Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20, 2026, leverage this valuable moment to fine-tune sustainability strategies. It’s an excellent opportunity to test current priorities against emerging policy signals, market expectations and practical solutions, then seize those insights for value creation pathways.
5 ways to strengthen corporate sustainability strategies
Consider the following when evaluating sustainability strategies:
1. Start with the sustainability narrative relevant to your company
There is no universal sustainability storyline.
A financial institution may focus on financing the energy transition, helping customers manage risk and supporting resilient communities. A manufacturer may focus on energy, materials, waste, product design and workforce skills. A technology company may need to discuss data-centre energy use, responsible AI, digital inclusion and the people who train and oversee its systems.
When building an ESG communication strategy, “How can we sound sustainable?” is the wrong question.
Ask questions that authentically uncover your organization’s story:
- What impact does our business have?
- What do we depend on from people, communities and the natural environment?
- Where are we making progress?
- Where are we still exposed?
- What decisions are changing because of what we have learned?
The best sustainability narrative is connected to the actual business. It needs to explain why the issue is material to the company, its stakeholders and the future it helps create.
2. Listen to your Ganeshes
Every organization has people who understand risks before they become an ice shelf drifting toward Europe. They may work in sustainability, environmental health and safety, risk, compliance, operations, employee relations, social impact or community engagement.
Consider their insights, even when the recommendation is more difficult, more expensive or something the company has never done before.
Welcome the feedback sustainability professionals offer when they say:
- This claim is too broad.
- Our data does not support this target.
- This project affects a community differently than we assumed.
- This technology creates a new risk.
- We need to consult people earlier.
- We cannot solve this with a marketing campaign.
Those interventions can feel frustrating, particularly when an organization is under pressure to move quickly. But expertise that complicates a decision can prevent a much larger future problem.
Ganesh struggles in his role despite his knowledge, skill, or experience—presumably the reasons why he was hired. He appears ineffective because power, convenience and self-interest repeatedly subordinate his mandate. With Ganesh at the table, companies can establish governance that brings sustainability expertise to decision-makers early and elevates the credibility of outputs as a source of strategic value creation.
3. Treat engagement as part of the work
A company does not need to attend every climate and sustainability conference. But it should understand that engagement with policymakers, regulators, investors, researchers, communities and peers is part of sustainability work.
COP31 will provide companies, investors, entrepreneurs and innovators the opportunity to connect around scalable climate solutions, clean technologies, sustainable industry and public-private partnerships.
Many companies have discussed at length if attending is worth the cost, time and logistical effort. Not every organization needs to send a large delegation, but low corporate engagement has its own cost.
If companies don’t bring operational knowledge to the table, policymakers may design rules without enough insight into how they’ll be implemented. If governments and regulators do not hear business realities, companies may struggle to act at scale. If companies stay away, they also miss opportunities to understand where policy, markets, and expectations are heading.
COP31 is a notable venue for that engagement, but it’s definitely not the only one. Find the right forums to execute a COP-aligned strategy where it makes the most sense.
Before any engagement, companies should define what they need to learn and what they can contribute. That might include operational data, lessons from a pilot project, workforce-transition experience, financing barriers or insight into what would make a regulation more workable.
4. Communicate about progress and transition
Sustainability has no finish line. Goals will keep moving as technology changes, regulations evolve, supply chains mature and ways of working shift.
A company that reaches an emissions target is not finished. A company that introduces AI is not finished. A company that improves its workplace practices is not finished.
The more credible message is one of progress and transition: We have improved in these areas. We are still working through these problems. Here is what we have learned, and here is what we will do next.
Disclosing unanticipated challenges is not an admission of failure. It is an honest account of how responsible business works.
A sustainable narrative can follow a simple structure:
- Here was our starting point.
- Here is what we changed.
- Here is the impact so far.
- Here is what remains difficult.
- Here is how our next phase will be different.
This approach tells a story that can develop with the business.
5. Put people and communities at the centre
Keeping communities employed is another opportunity to strengthen sustainability. Jobs support households, local businesses, public services, skills, and social stability. Transformation that doesn’t consider people’s livelihoods will not feel sustainable to the people living through it.
Companies should normalize telling the full story of how they support employees and the communities where they operate:
- What skills are being developed?
- Which jobs are being retained or redesigned?
- How are workers being supported through technological change?
- How are local suppliers and small businesses included?
- How is knowledge being transferred between generations?

articles.summary: Biodiversity loss also affects insurance  Web corporativa - Mapfre
articles.full_text:
For decades, biodiversity has been considered a matter reserved almost exclusively to the field of environmental conservation. However, that approach has changed radically and today occupies a priority place on the agendas of European financial supervisors, who are scrutinizing how the degradation of nature can alter the value of investments and increase the cost of insured claims.
Through European Directive 2025/2, which revised the Solvency II framework, the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) was entrusted with a very specific task: analyzing to what extent companies evaluate their exposure to these types of contingencies. The resulting report, published on June 30, 2025, marks the first official assessment by European supervisory authorities of how the sector manages these risks. The Solvency II framework already requires insurance companies to integrate sustainability risks, including biodiversity, into their governance and their internal risk assessment. The document also outlines some of the practices currently used across the sector as a diagnostic tool to help companies better understand the risk.
The starting point of the document leaves no room for doubt, stating that if ecological deterioration continues to advance, the economic consequences could be severe, even threatening the stability of the global financial system. This issue directly affects asset valuations while also influencing the frequency and severity of claims across the market.
More than half of global GDP depends on natural resources. In addition, water-related problems could reduce global GDP by 7% to 9%, with the manufacturing industry particularly hard hit. In agriculture, 14% to 18% of production could be at risk due to water-related issues, while pollinator decline could put up to 12% at risk. For its part, the World Economic Forum places this deterioration among the main threats to the economy over a ten-year horizon.
In its analysis of assets, EIOPA found that nearly 30% of direct investments in corporate bonds and equities are highly dependent on water or other ecosystem resources. However, these figures should be interpreted with caution. While high dependency indicates vulnerability, the actual impact on capital varies depending on the measures taken by each company.
On the liability side, environmental changes affect several types of coverage offered by insurance companies. The loss of wetlands, for example, reduces natural protection against disasters, increasing claims for property damage and business interruption. Similarly, soil degradation affects crop insurance performance, while declining pollinator populations reduce the productivity of insured crops. Rising zoonotic disease rates affect health-related lines of business, while water pollution leads to environmental responsibility claims. An analysis by the Sustainable Insurance Forum indicates that seven economic sectors, responsible for nearly 10% of global property and casualty insurance premiums, could face significant disruptions if these risks worsen. Conversely, nature acts as an effective shield: forest diversity slows the spread of wildfires, while marshes help absorb the force of storms.
Quantifying these phenomena, however, remains a challenge. A review of more than 700 internal assessments for 2023 revealed that only one in five companies mentioned biodiversity, with the proportion doubling among larger firms. When this analysis is undertaken, it is generally based on qualitative assessments, with purely quantitative models being rare. Most companies consider biodiversity an important but emerging risk that is difficult to translate into tangible financial impacts. The biggest obstacles lie in the scarcity of standardized data and in the territorial complexity of a problem linked to climate change. Such scarcity also restricts the overall view of the industry’s exposure in underwriting.
Despite these limitations, EIOPA highlights the existence of pioneering methodologies in agriculture, real estate, and health. A clear example is that of the Dutch insurance company a.s.r., which calculated that 16.5% of its property and casualty business is located near Natura 2000 sites, estimating that 3% of its corporate clients have a significant impact on the environment. Among the measures identified by EIOPA are sectoral or geographic exclusions and the financing of nature-based solutions.
At the regulatory level, the EU Biodiversity Strategy aims to provide legal protection to 30% of European territory by 2030, while the Nature Restoration Law requires restoration measures to be implemented across 20% of these areas. Following the report, EIOPA plans to develop targeted training programs for both supervisors and the industry.
In the private sector, notable initiatives include that of Mapfre, which approved its Corporate Natural Capital Framework in 2025. The company offset 45,136 metric tons of carbon dioxide through forestry and clean energy projects, covering 84% of its operational carbon footprint. These initiatives are selected based on their ability to prevent flooding and wildfires, as well as their positive impact on pollinators. In addition, the company’s volunteer activities recorded 3,532 participations across 207 events in 23 countries, resulting in the planting of 5,877 trees and the removal of 7,857 kilograms of waste from natural environments.

articles.title: Baguio Embraces Circular Economy for Sustainable Festivals and Celebrations - Daily Tribune
articles.summary: Baguio Embraces Circular Economy for Sustainable Festivals and Celebrations  Daily Tribune
articles.full_text:
BAGUIO CITY — The city government is integrating its "Pansa-nopen Tayo" circular economy program into major public celebrations, including the Ibag-iw Creative Festival this November and Christmas festivities in December, to reduce waste and promote sustainable practices.
Mayor Benjamin Magalong said the initiative encourages residents and visitors to view discarded materials as resources that can be reused, recycled or transformed into functional and creative products.
The program, rooted in the Ibaloi concept of gathering, conserving and reusing resources, seeks to replace the traditional "take-make-dispose" approach with more sustainable waste management practices.
ADVERTISEMENT
The city first incorporated circular economy measures into the Baguio Flower Festival, or Panagbenga, in February.
During the festival, organizers implemented improved waste collection and segregation systems, promoted recyclable cutlery and provided filtered water stations to reduce the use of single-use plastic bottles.
The Baguio Flower Festival Foundation Inc. also partnered with private groups to encourage waste segregation and the exchange of recyclable materials.
ADVERTISEMENT
City Tourism Officer Aloysius Mapalo said the initiative was carried over to the city's 117th Charter Day celebration in September, which adopted the theme "Everlasting Baguio: Cultivating Circularity."
The same approach will be highlighted during the Ibag-iw Creative Festival, which will feature contemporary artworks made from scrap materials by students under the guidance of professional artists.
An exhibition of recycled crafts and a musical production titled "Rikus," exploring the concept of circularity in Cordilleran culture, are also part of the festival's activities.
For the Christmas celebrations, the city government has commissioned local artists to create holiday decorations and installations using repurposed materials instead of relying heavily on commercially produced ornaments.
The initiative aims to minimize waste while providing opportunities for local artists to showcase their creativity.
Baguio has also institutionalized its circular economy framework through City Ordinance No. 15, series of 2026, which promotes resource efficiency, waste reduction and sustainable development.
The city government hopes the integration of these practices into public celebrations will encourage residents, businesses and tourists to adopt environmentally responsible habits beyond major events.

articles.title: Indian Beverage Association’s Dr Gunveena Chadha on EPR, Plastic Recycling and Circular Economy in India - The CSR Universe
articles.summary: Indian Beverage Association’s Dr Gunveena Chadha on EPR, Plastic Recycling and Circular Economy in India  The CSR Universe
articles.full_text:
India’s expanding beverage market brings with it a growing responsibility to address packaging waste, resource consumption and the environmental costs of production. As circular economy principles gain prominence in policy discussions, the focus is increasingly shifting from regulatory compliance to building systems that can deliver measurable improvements in resource efficiency, waste recovery and recycling. The BRICS New Delhi Declaration’s emphasis on Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), eco-design and sustainable waste management adds an important dimension to this conversation, particularly for industries with significant packaging footprints. For India’s non-alcoholic beverage sector, this presents both an opportunity and a challenge: translating commitments into effective collection systems, greater use of recycled materials and stronger accountability across the value chain. In this interview with TheCSRUniverse, Dr Gunveena Chadha, Secretary General, Indian Beverage Association (IBA), discusses the industry's progress, persistent implementation gaps, the role of policy and consumer participation, and the priorities that will shape its transition towards a more circular and resource-efficient future.
Read the full interview below:
Q. India’s beverage industry is growing alongside rising consumption and increasing concerns around packaging waste. How can the sector balance growth with its environmental responsibilities and make sustainability an integral part of its business practices?
A. India’s non-alcoholic ready-to-drink beverage (NARTD) industry is integrating sustainability into its growth strategy through lightweight packaging, resource-efficient operations and stronger recycling systems. By going beyond regulatory compliance and adopting circular practices, the sector aims to reduce its environmental footprint. Achieving this requires continued collaboration among industry, government and consumers.
The NARTD beverage industry recognises that growth and sustainability must advance together. As consumer demand rises, the sector is increasingly investing in packaging innovation, circular economy partnerships and efficient use of resources to reduce environmental impact across the value chain. This includes expanding the use of recyclable materials, increasing recycled content in packaging, improving collection and recovery systems, and supporting infrastructure that enables waste segregation and recycling at scale. Water stewardship, energy efficiency and lower-emission manufacturing are also becoming central priorities as companies work to build more resilient and responsible supply chains.
Making sustainability integral to business practices will require strong collaboration among industry, government, recyclers and consumers. Clear policy frameworks, investment in recycling infrastructure and wider adoption of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) mechanisms can help accelerate systemic change. At the same time, consumer awareness and participation remain essential to improving collection and recycling outcomes. Sustainability can no longer be treated as a parallel initiative; it must be embedded into product design, operations, sourcing and long-term business strategy. By combining innovation with collective action, India’s beverage sector can continue to meet growing demand while contributing meaningfully to environmental progress and circularity.
Q. The BRICS New Delhi Declaration places emphasis on circular economy, EPR and sustainable waste management. What opportunities does this create for India’s beverage industry, and how can these commitments translate into measurable outcomes?
A. The BRICS Declaration reinforces the importance of a circular economy and provides strong opportunities to accelerate circularity through knowledge-sharing, packaging innovation and collaboration on recycling technologies. Its emphasis on Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR), eco-design and sustainable waste management practices aligns with ongoing industry initiatives. These efforts can strengthen recovery infrastructure, improve traceability and encourage greater use of recycled materials. This can encourage greater investment in recycling infrastructure, packaging innovation and the use of recycled content, while also supporting the formalisation of the waste value chain and creating livelihood opportunities for waste workers and recyclers.
To translate these commitments into measurable outcomes, collaboration across industry, government and civil society will be essential. Clear and achievable targets for collection and recycling, improved traceability and reporting systems, and investments in circular infrastructure can help drive accountability and progress. With a balanced approach that combines policy support, innovation and shared responsibility, the beverage industry can help advance India’s circular economy ambitions while delivering tangible environmental and economic benefits.
Q. How much progress has the beverage industry made in reducing its packaging footprint through lightweighting, redesign and recycling? What key challenges remain?
A. The NARTD beverage industry has made significant progress in reducing its packaging footprint through lightweighting, redesign and a greater focus on recyclability. Companies are using less material in packaging, improving transportation efficiency, increasing recyclable formats and incorporating more recycled content. Many are also supporting collection and recovery systems as part of their broader sustainability and EPR commitments.
At the same time, challenges remain in scaling up these efforts across India. Recycling infrastructure and waste collection systems are uneven across regions, while consumer awareness and waste segregation need improvement. The industry is challenged to balance sustainability goals with affordability, product safety and supply chain realities. Continued collaboration among industry, government, recyclers and communities will be critical to achieving long-term circularity and measurable environmental impact.
Q. While EPR has encouraged companies to take greater responsibility for packaging waste, its success depends on effective collection and recycling systems. Where are the biggest gaps in implementation, and how can industry and government work together to address them?
A. Fragmented waste collection and inadequate source segregation remain significant challenges. Industry and government can address these gaps by strengthening collection networks and infrastructure. Standardised municipal procedures across the country and closer coordination with local authorities can also make EPR implementation more efficient.
Q. What is the industry's approach to increasing the use of recycled materials and exploring alternative packaging? What are the key barriers to making these solutions viable at scale?
A. The beverage industry is increasingly focused on expanding the use of food-grade recycled materials, especially recycled PET approved by the Food Safety Authority, as part of its commitment to circular packaging solutions. These recycling processes are already approved by European and American authorities for their safe use as food-contact materials. Companies are also exploring alternative packaging formats and material innovations that can help reduce dependence on virgin resources while maintaining product safety, quality and consumer trust.
However, scaling these solutions remains challenging. One of the key barriers is the limited availability of food-grade recycled material at the quality and volumes required for large-scale beverage production. While collection, segregation and recycling infrastructure continue to grow, there is still room to further enhance these aspects to ensure enough food-grade recycled material is made available for the entire industry. Addressing these challenges will require coordinated action across industry, government, recyclers and consumers to build a stronger and more efficient circular economy ecosystem.
Q. What steps can the industry take to ensure greater transparency and traceability in waste collection and recycling?
A. Digital platforms can track plastic waste from collection to processing, creating audit-ready records and improving traceability. Partnerships with Producer Responsibility Organisations (PROs), digital weight verification and reliable reporting can strengthen accountability.
Q. How can beverage companies encourage responsible disposal and waste segregation among consumers?
A. Companies are encouraging responsible disposal by making waste segregation convenient and accessible through clear packaging instructions, collection points and community initiatives. Sustained engagement and awareness campaigns are essential. Collaboration with local governments, waste collectors and civil society can help make responsible disposal a regular consumer habit.
Q. What opportunities does the proposed BRICS knowledge-sharing network offer, and what are IBA's sustainability priorities for the next three to five years?
A. The proposed BRICS knowledge-sharing network offers opportunities to exchange best practices and accelerate packaging and recycling innovation. Over the next three to five years, priorities include lightweight packaging, stronger digital collection networks and expanded food-grade r-PET manufacturing. Collaboration among industry, government and consumers will remain essential to advancing circularity.

articles.title: The European Union Deforestation Regulation’s Uneven Impact: Who Is Exposed and What Are the Costs? - Impakter
articles.summary: The European Union Deforestation Regulation’s Uneven Impact: Who Is Exposed and What Are the Costs?  Impakter
articles.full_text:
For decades, agricultural expansion has driven deforestation worldwide. According to the EUDR’s preamble, the European Union imported and consumed a third of the globally traded agricultural products associated with deforestation between 1990 and 2008, and its consumption was responsible for 10% of worldwide deforestation associated with the production of goods or services over that period. In response, the bloc adopted the EUDR to reduce its contribution to global deforestation and forest degradation.The law covers seven commodities: cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber, soya, and wood, along with a list of derived products. To be placed on or exported from the EU market, these goods must be (i) deforestation-free, (ii) legally produced, and (iii) covered by a due diligence statement.
Although the EUDR targets EU consumption, its effects will be felt well beyond the bloc’s borders. Who is actually exposed? And who will bear the cost of compliance? Understanding what the EUDR will change means looking at several factors together: countries’ exports to the European Union, the bloc’s own import patterns, how deforestation risk is assessed, and what the regulation requires of different actors along the value chain.
The EUDR’s evolving rules and risk classification
The EUDR has evolved significantly since its adoption. Its timing, product scope, and obligations have changed repeatedly since adoption, and each change affects which goods are covered, who must carry out due diligence, and how much compliance costs. The country risk classification, which determines how closely imports from each country are checked, is also subject to periodic review.
The regulation entered into force in June 2023, but its application date has been postponed twice, most recently to December 30, 2026 (June 30, 2027, for most micro and small operators). A December 2025 amendment simplified the rules, shifting the due diligence obligation to the first operator placing a product on the EU market and introducing a simplified regime for micro and small primary operators. Most recently, the European Commission adopted Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/2102 in July 2026, amending the list of covered products to remove certain products, such as cattle hides, skins, and leather, and to add products such as soluble coffee and certain palm oil derivatives. The regulation will apply to these products from December 30, 2027.
The European Commission also published updated guidance in July 2026 to reflect the December 2025 amendments, clarifying the obligations of downstream operators and of micro and small primary operators. In its May 2026 simplification review, the European Commission stated that it does not consider it appropriate to propose further amendments to the regulation itself, although the country classification will be reviewed periodically and guidance may continue to be updated. This analysis reflects the rules as they stand at the time of writing.
Three perspectives on the EUDR’s impact
Exporters: Which countries are most economically exposed?
By size, Brazil and China are the European Union’s two largest suppliers, accounting for 14.7% and 14.4% of EUDR-covered imports respectively (see figure below). Brazil’s exports span soya, coffee, wood, and cattle, while China’s are mainly wood and rubber products. These two economies are most exposed in terms of the actual volumes of trade of covered goods.
Measured by dependence, however, the picture reverses. Both Brazil and China export large volumes of other goods, so EUDR-covered sales to the European Union account for only a small part of their total exports: about 5% for Brazil and even less for China, which does not appear among the 10 most-exposed countries (see figure below). For a group of smaller exporters, the share is far higher. EUDR-covered goods sold to the European Union account for half of São Tomé and Príncipe’s total exports, mostly cocoa and palm oil. Burundi, Côte d’Ivoire, and Cameroon each rely on EUDR-covered goods sold to the European Union for at least a quarter of their total export value. Across the most exposed countries, dependence is usually concentrated in a single commodity: coffee in Burundi, Ethiopia, Rwanda, and Uganda, and cocoa in Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, Ghana, and Sierra Leone.
For these countries, a high share shows that much of their export value depends on EU buyers being able to document that products are deforestation-free and legally produced. If a supply chain cannot provide that information, EU buyers may drop it, or the trade may be redirected to other markets. The measure is therefore an indicator of exposure, not an estimate of losses.
The European Union: How much of the bloc’s trade is affected?
EUDR products represent a relatively small share of EU imports from outside the EU, but there is substantial concentration in particular commodities and origins.
EUDR-covered commodities accounted for around 4.3% of the European Union’s imports in 2024, but this share is not evenly dispersed. Wood alone makes up a third (35%) of those imports, while rubber, cocoa, coffee, and soya contribute roughly 13%–14%, oil palm 8%, and cattle only 2%.
That concentration deepens at the country level. For several commodities, a single country supplies over a third of the European Union’s total imports, including cocoa from Côte d’Ivoire and coffee from Brazil. Indonesia supplies around 40% of the European Union’s oil palm products’ imports, and Brazil close to half of its soya imports (see figure below).
From the European Union’s point of view, the regulation covers a manageable share of total trade, concentrated in a few product lines. But that concentration also creates vulnerability. Because the supply of commodities like cocoa and soya depends heavily on a small number of countries, a compliance problem in just one of them could affect a large share of the European Union’s supply of that commodity, even though the commodity itself represents only a small share of total EU trade.
Operators: What does EUDR compliance cost, and who will pay?
Even if aggregate compliance costs have fallen following simplification, those costs and adjustment pressures may be unevenly distributed across operators, exporters, and producers.
The compliance burden of the EUDR depends heavily on two things: the country risk classification and what the regulation requires of actors along the value chain. Under Article 29, the European Commission assigns every country one of three tiers: low, standard, or high risk. This classification reflects the European Union’s assessment of deforestation risk under its own criteria. The figure below shows the current classification.
The classification rests primarily on quantitative criteria: the rate of net forest area loss, drawn from the United Nations (UN) Food and Agriculture Organization’s Forest Resource Assessment (FAO FRA), and the rate of expansion of agricultural land or production for the seven regulated commodities, from FAOSTAT. A country qualifies as low risk if it meets any one of three conditions: it recorded no net forest loss between 2015 and 2020, its average annual forest area loss stayed below set relative and absolute thresholds, or it showed no expansion of cropland, livestock production, or overall agricultural land linked to the regulated commodities. Countries close to these thresholds undergo a second, more qualitative review that considers factors such as the strength of a country’s forest governance and its cooperation with the European Union. The regulation requires the list to be reviewed as often as necessary in light of new evidence, and the European Commission has said it envisages a first review in 2026, following the publication of updated FAO FRA data.
The risk tier determines whether operators can use simplified due diligence. It also sets, under Article 16, the minimum share of operators that competent authorities must check: at least 1% for products from low-risk countries, 3% for standard-risk countries, and 9% for high-risk countries. Half of the 20 most exposed countries are officially rated low risk under Article 29, including São Tomé and Príncipe, Burundi, Ghana, and Rwanda. Products from these countries are eligible for simplified due diligence, although their high dependence on the European Union market means that the regulation still applies to a large share of their export value. However, several highly dependent countries are rated standard risk, including Côte d’Ivoire and Cameroon, where EUDR-covered sales to the EU account for around a quarter of total exports, as well as Ethiopia, Uganda, Sierra Leone, Honduras, and Liberia. Operators sourcing from these countries must carry out full due diligence, so these countries combine high dependence on the EU market with the full set of information requirements. None of the 20 most exposed countries are rated high risk.
A European Commission report from May 2026 estimates that businesses’ annual compliance costs will total around EUR 2.0 billion, down from an estimated EUR 8.1 billion before the simplifications, a reduction of around 75%. The report sets these costs against an estimated EUR 7 billion a year in economic benefits from avoided deforestation and greenhouse gas emissions. These costs, however, will not be evenly distributed along value chains.

This distinction is important because a producer is not necessarily an operator. Producers that sell their products to intermediaries, rather than placing products on the EU market or exporting them from the European Union themselves, have no direct obligations under the regulation.

Financial and Structural Barriers
The Welsh public sector is highly unlikely to achieve the government's ambition of reaching net zero carbon emissions by 2030, hindered by severe financial pressures, skills shortages and a lack of coordinated action, according to a stark new assessment by Audit Wales. The findings raise significant questions about the viability of Wales' climate commitments, revealing that decarbonization has increasingly been sidelined by competing spending priorities.
The Welsh Government declared a climate emergency in 2019 and established a collective ambition for the public sector to achieve net zero by 2030, positioning public organizations as leaders in the transition to a low-carbon economy. However, Audit Wales found that progress has been insufficient, with climate considerations failing to become fully embedded into everyday decision-making across the sector.
Data Quality and Workforce Challenges
Financial constraints represent the most formidable barrier; decarbonizing Welsh council buildings alone is estimated to cost at least £2.3 billion, a figure that public bodies describe as unaffordable amid current budget pressures. The report also identified critical weaknesses in how carbon emissions are measured and reported, particularly regarding supply chain emissions, cautioning that recent increases in reported emissions partly reflect improved data coverage rather than solely deteriorating performance.
| Key Barriers to Welsh Public Sector Net Zero |  | 
|---|---|
| Barrier Category | Primary Impact | 
|---|---|
| Financial Pressures | Decarbonization sidelined by immediate operational demands | 
| Skills Shortages | Heavy reliance on external consultants for program delivery | 
| Data Quality | Inaccurate tracking of supply chain and Scope 3 emissions | 
Workforce capability remains a persistent obstacle, with public bodies citing severe shortages in the specialist skills required to plan and execute complex decarbonization programs. Ann-Marie Harkin, Executive Director for Audit Delivery at Audit Wales, noted that while the ambition was intended to catalyze wider economic changes, "not enough progress has been made overall," emphasizing the urgent need for realistic financial planning and capacity building.
Recommendations for the Welsh Government
- Strategic Clarity: Provide clearer guidance on prioritizing decarbonization against competing statutory obligations.
- Financial Support: Develop realistic, long-term funding models to support infrastructure upgrades across local authorities and health boards.
- Reporting Standards: Improve the accuracy and consistency of carbon emissions reporting, particularly for complex supply chains.
- Workforce Development: Invest in training programs to build internal capacity for energy management and low-carbon project delivery.
The findings have broader implications for the Welsh economy, particularly for businesses in construction, renewable energy and environmental services that depend on a predictable pipeline of public sector infrastructure projects. With just four years remaining until the 2030 deadline, the report concludes that achieving meaningful progress will require a fundamental shift toward delivery-focused execution and closer collaboration between government, public institutions and the private sector.

articles.title: The Rise of Sustainability Reporting: Why Companies Are Turning to ESG Consultants and Outsourcing Partners - Business News This Week
articles.summary: The Rise of Sustainability Reporting: Why Companies Are Turning to ESG Consultants and Outsourcing Partners  Business News This Week
articles.full_text:
Nov 03: Sustainability is becoming a business issue that companies can no longer address through commitments and policy statements alone. Investors want measurable information about environmental performance, corporate customers are reviewing supplier practices, and regulators are introducing more structured disclosure requirements. As a result, businesses are paying greater attention to how they measure, document and communicate their sustainability performance.
This change is creating demand for a specialised range of professional services. Companies need help with everything from measuring carbon emissions and collecting environmental data to preparing sustainability reports and understanding regulatory requirements.
For large organisations, these responsibilities can involve several departments and multiple business locations. Smaller businesses face a different challenge: they may not have the resources to employ dedicated ESG professionals or invest in specialised reporting systems.
Consequently, ESG consulting firms, accounting service providers and business process outsourcing (BPO) companies are finding new opportunities in sustainability reporting.
What makes this development particularly interesting is that the demand extends beyond report preparation. Businesses increasingly need year-round assistance with data collection, performance monitoring, compliance documentation and reporting systems. This could make sustainability services an important growth area for the global professional services and outsourcing industries.
Why Businesses Are Paying Greater Attention to ESG Reporting
Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) reporting provides stakeholders with information about how companies manage their environmental impact, employees, business practices and corporate responsibilities.
Several developments are driving its adoption.
Investors are increasingly interested in understanding how climate-related risks, energy costs, resource availability and governance practices could influence a company’s future performance. Sustainability information can help them assess risks that may not be immediately visible in traditional financial statements.
Supply chain expectations are another important factor. Large corporations are asking their suppliers to provide information about emissions, energy consumption, waste management and labour practices. Businesses seeking international contracts may therefore need to demonstrate their sustainability practices even if they are not directly subject to mandatory ESG reporting.
Regulatory developments are also influencing corporate behaviour. The International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB), established by the IFRS Foundation, introduced IFRS S1 and IFRS S2 to provide a global baseline for sustainability-related financial disclosures.
In Europe, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS) have established a framework for corporate sustainability disclosures. However, the regulatory landscape has continued to evolve, with the European Union introducing simplification measures to reduce reporting requirements and administrative costs.
For businesses operating across multiple markets, understanding these different requirements is becoming an important management responsibility. This is creating opportunities for ESG consultants who can help companies interpret reporting standards and develop suitable compliance processes.
The Growing Complexity of Sustainability Data
Preparing an ESG report involves collecting information from several areas of a business. Unlike conventional financial information, sustainability data is often spread across departments, facilities and external suppliers.
A manufacturing company, for example, may need to track electricity consumption, fuel usage, water consumption, waste generation and transportation-related emissions. It may also need information about the environmental practices of its suppliers.
The human resources department may maintain records relating to employee welfare, workplace safety and diversity, while the finance and compliance teams handle governance-related information.
Bringing these records together requires consistent reporting methods and coordination between departments.
Carbon accounting adds another layer of complexity. Companies may need to measure three categories of greenhouse gas emissions:
- Scope 1: Direct emissions from sources owned or controlled by the company.
- Scope 2: Indirect emissions associated with purchased electricity, heating and cooling.
- Scope 3: Other indirect emissions generated across the company’s value chain.
Scope 3 reporting can be particularly demanding because it requires information from suppliers, transport providers and other external partners.
For businesses with international supply chains, gathering reliable information from multiple sources can become a continuous task. Incomplete records or inconsistent calculations can also affect the quality of the final disclosure.
This is one reason companies are looking beyond their existing finance and administrative teams for specialised ESG reporting support.
Why Companies Are Hiring ESG Consultants
ESG consultants are helping businesses understand their reporting responsibilities and develop systems to manage sustainability-related information.
Their role is not limited to preparing annual reports. They can work with management teams to identify important ESG issues, assess existing practices and establish processes for monitoring performance.
Some of the key services offered by ESG consulting firms include:
ESG compliance and regulatory guidance: Businesses need to understand which reporting standards apply to their operations. Consultants help interpret relevant requirements, identify gaps and develop appropriate disclosure procedures.
Carbon accounting and emissions measurement: Companies looking to reduce their environmental footprint first need to understand where their emissions originate. Consultants help establish measurement systems, calculate carbon footprints and identify opportunities for improvement.
Sustainability strategy: ESG specialists help businesses assess environmental and social risks and incorporate relevant considerations into corporate planning.
Supply chain sustainability: Companies increasingly need to evaluate their suppliers’ environmental and labour practices. Consultants can help establish assessment procedures and monitor potential risks.
Reporting and assurance readiness: Businesses need supporting documentation and reliable internal controls. Consultants help organise information and prepare companies for independent assurance where applicable.
For organisations entering ESG reporting for the first time, these services can provide access to expertise without requiring them to develop every capability internally.
Why Sustainability Reporting Outsourcing Is Gaining Momentum
While ESG consultants often focus on strategy and technical guidance, outsourcing partners can take on much of the operational work involved in sustainability reporting.
Establishing an in-house ESG department requires investment in recruitment, training, software and reporting infrastructure. This may not be practical for companies that need specialised support but do not have sufficient ongoing requirements to maintain a large internal team.
Sustainability reporting outsourcing offers an alternative. Companies can engage external service providers to manage specific reporting activities or support the process throughout the year.
These services may include:
- ESG data collection and consolidation.
- Carbon emissions data processing.

ESG Rating Providers Face FCA Authorisation From June 2027 Under New Conflict-of-Interest Rules
- Applications open 2027: ESG rating providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027.
- Four rule areas: The framework sets requirements on transparency, governance, systems and controls, and conflicts of interest.
- Scope guidance published: The FCA has issued guidance so firms can check whether their ESG ratings or assessments fall in scope.
The UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) will regulate ESG rating providers for the first time under a new framework. ESG stands for environmental, social and governance. The regime applies to firms or organisations that provide ESG ratings and assessments. Providers operating in the UK market will need to apply for FCA authorisation from 24 June 2027.
The framework introduces requirements covering transparency, governance, systems and controls, and the management of conflicts of interest. According to the FCA, the rules are proportionate to each firm’s size and activities. They also draw on international and existing standards. However, the FCA did not specify when the full regime takes effect, the penalties for breaches or any size thresholds.
The FCA said the rules aim to improve the transparency, reliability and comparability of ESG ratings. It added that the ratings market plays an important role in investment decisions. Higher standards should help investors make better informed decisions, the regulator said. “Trusted information is essential for well-functioning markets. These rules will help improve transparency and raise standards across the ESG ratings market while supporting competition, innovation and growth,” said Laura Dawes, director of authorisations and sustainable finance at the FCA.

What Firms Must Do Now
The FCA urged firms that may be in scope to start preparing now. It told them to check whether the framework applies to their activities and to review the final rules and guidance. Firms should also consider whether they need authorisation, begin implementation work and engage early with FCA support services. “Firms should check now whether they are in scope and start preparing for authorisation. We’ll continue to provide practical support to help them prepare,” Dawes said.
Who It Affects
- UK ESG rating providers: Can join FCA webinars and use its Pre-Application Support Service to prepare before applications open.
- Firms offering ESG assessments: Providers of ESG assessments, not only formal ratings, may be in scope and should check the FCA’s guidance.
- Ratings users and rated companies: Providers must engage with both the users of their ESG ratings and the entities they rate

articles.full_text:
Carbon Gap Launches Free Carbon Removal Toolkit for Governments
- Free open-access toolkit: Carbon Gap has released a free toolkit for estimating a country’s realistic carbon removal potential.
- Tested methodology: The toolkit packages a methodology refined over two years and applied in seven countries.
- COP31 presentation: Carbon Gap will present the toolkit to national delegations at the Think Negative Pavilion at COP31.
Carbon Gap has launched a free, open-access toolkit for estimating how much carbon dioxide removal (CDR) a country could realistically deliver. It packages the methodology that Carbon Gap and its local partners refined over two years and used in seven countries. The toolkit sits on the new Carbon Removal Readiness Assessment (CRRA) website, alongside every CRRA published to date.
According to Carbon Gap, most countries have a net-zero target, but few know how much carbon they could remove at home. Few also know which removal methods suit them best or what policies would be needed. Each CRRA starts by mapping a country’s resources, such as land, energy, minerals and geological storage. It then tests that physical potential against national policy, stakeholder views and public opinion to build realistic scenarios.
What the Toolkit Includes
The toolkit lets governments, researchers and civil society organisations run the same assessment for their own country. It includes a step-by-step guide covering the methodology, timelines, budgets and staffing. “For two years we’ve been asking the same question, one country at a time: how much carbon could you actually remove? Now we’re handing over the recipe. Any government, university, or NGO can pick up this toolkit and get a credible answer for their own country, autonomously,” said Sylvain Delerce, Chief Scientist at Carbon Gap.
Users also get templates for the background report and the national roadmap, plus materials for stakeholder interviews and citizen panels. A taxonomy of CDR methods and a database of resource requirements were developed with RMI. Meanwhile, an optimisation tool models how a country’s resources could be efficiently allocated across CDR methods. Carbon Gap did not name the seven countries assessed or any government committed to using the toolkit.
Why It Matters
The toolkit turns Carbon Gap’s country-by-country assessment work into a resource that governments can run without its direct involvement. It also gives Carbon Gap a ready product for national delegations at COP31, held in Antalya from 9 to 20 November. If delegations adopt it, Carbon Gap’s method could underpin national carbon removal roadmaps beyond its first seven assessments.

articles.summary:

The post COP30 Presidency Lays Out 2033 Fossil Fuel Transition, Forest Finance Roadmaps appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
COP30 Presidency Lays Out 2033 Fossil Fuel Transition, Forest Finance Roadmaps
- Energy timeline: Countries would replace fossil fuels from 2031 to 2033.
- Forest fund: Brazil’s forest facility has $7.6 billion of a $10 billion target.
- Implementation call: Correa do Lago says governments must act, not renegotiate.
Brazil is ending its year-long presidency of the UN climate process with roadmaps for governments on fossil fuels and deforestation. Under the energy roadmap, countries would draft transition plans by 2028 and replace fossil fuels from 2031 to 2033. Reuters did not report an enforcement mechanism or which countries endorse the roadmaps.
Andre Correa do Lago, COP30 President, led last November’s UN climate summit in Belem and said governments must integrate climate goals into policymaking. “We don’t need more negotiations. What we need is for governments to start taking action,” Correa do Lago told Reuters. “We need to completely change the way governments deal with climate change. To implement this, we need finance, infrastructure and transportation ministers at the table.”
Quick anonymous worklife pollWhat's my daily work emissions burn, or savings?Powered by ESG News
COP31 opens in Antalya, southern Turkey, on November 9. Murat Kurum is the summit president and Turkish environment, urbanisation and climate change minister. In September, he told the UN the agenda would also focus on implementation rather than new pledges, based on “dialogue, consensus and action.”
Fossil Fuel Roadmap
In Belem, the roadmap had European support but failed to win consensus after opposition from major oil-producing countries. Before 2028, countries would assess energy systems and strengthen regulations ahead of the second Global Stocktake, a UN review of climate progress.
By 2030, infrastructure upgrades and renewable investments should be underway. Global renewable capacity hit a record 5,149 gigawatts at the end of 2025, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. Yet Brazil’s roadmap notes most recent growth met new demand rather than replacing fossil fuels. “My opinion is that it doesn’t need to be negotiated again because that negotiation has already taken place,” said Correa do Lago. “It needs to be implemented.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Schneider Electric Backs Brazil’s Industrial Decarbonization push at COP30
Forest Finance Roadmap
Disagreement over forest finance also kept the deforestation roadmap out of the final COP30 agreement. The United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) says annual forest funding must rise from $84.5 billion in 2023 to over $300 billion by 2030. National governments provide 88.3% of forest finance, while international public funding provides 3.4%.
Brazil’s Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF) would use sovereign fund returns to pay countries that preserve their forests. It had secured $7.6 billion against a $10 billion target by the end of COP30, according to Correa do Lago. The roadmap also backs stronger carbon markets, debt relief and direct finance for Indigenous peoples and local communities. “Public financing from developed countries is absolutely essential,” Correa do Lago said. “But we have a much more sophisticated and diversified way of financing the various activities that would reduce deforestation.” “It is not an easy task, and it is not just about financing. But financing is a central part of this process,” he added.
Who It Affects
- Oil-producing countries: The roadmap they opposed targets 2031 to 2033 for replacing fossil fuels.
- Developed countries: Correa do Lago calls their public financing essential to cutting deforestation.
- Tropical forest countries: Their national budgets carry most forest finance today, and TFFF payments depend on preserving forests.

Walmart Invests in Base Power, Offers 20% Off Home Battery Installs in Texas
- Strategic investment: Walmart has made a strategic investment in Base Power, a Texas-based home energy company.
- Installation discount: From November, eligible enrollees at participating Walmart and Sam’s Club locations get 20% off Base’s standard upfront installation fee.
- Texas launch: The offer starts in Texas, Base’s largest market, with expansion to more locations and markets expected over time.
Walmart has made a strategic investment in Base Power, a Texas-based energy company. Alongside the investment, an agreement makes Base’s home energy offerings available to Walmart customers and Sam’s Club members. Starting in November, eligible enrollees at participating stores get 20% off Base’s standard upfront battery installation fee. Base’s batteries are designed to lower energy costs while the grid is on and supply backup power when it is not.
Base installs, owns and maintains each home battery system, while customers pay an upfront installation fee. The company says that fee is a fraction of the cost of traditional whole-home backup solutions. “We’ve built Base around a simple idea: families deserve electricity that’s affordable when the grid is working and dependable backup power when it isn’t,” said Zach Dell, CEO of Base Power. “Walmart has been helping Americans save money and live better for more than 60 years. Base brings that same commitment to home energy, and we’re excited to do it together.”

In eligible areas of Texas, Base also sells electricity plans designed to help customers lower their bills. Walmart said the offerings can benefit both households and the grid. Product availability, savings potential, installation requirements and pricing vary by location, utility service area and customer circumstances. “Customers and members count on Walmart and Sam’s Club to help them make the most of their budgets,” said Shayne Wahlmeier, SVP of Walmart Energy. “Base Power gives them a practical way to help lower energy costs, have backup power during outages and support a more reliable grid. We’re proud to make these solutions more accessible through Walmart and Sam’s Club.”
Starting in Texas
Texas is Base’s largest and most established market, where it serves more than 35,000 members. More than 20,000 of those households have a Base battery at home, and the rest get their electricity from Base. Walmart is launching the offerings in Texas first and expects to expand to more locations and markets over time. articles.full_text:
Amazon UK Delivery Station Gets 6,400 Square Meters of CarbiCrete Cement-Free Paving
- First wide-scale deployment: CarbiCrete’s cement-free pavers now cover around 6,400 square meters of parking spaces and footpaths at Amazon’s new UK delivery station in Stockton-on-Tees.
- Low-carbon process: CarbiCrete replaces all cement with a steel-making by-product and cures its concrete with captured carbon dioxide.
- Certification target: The site is Amazon’s first building to pursue version 1.1 of Living Future’s Zero Carbon Certification.
CarbiCrete has supplied three cement-free concrete products to a new Amazon UK delivery station in Stockton-on-Tees. Its pavers now cover around 6,400 square meters of parking spaces and footpaths at the site. The company says this is the first wide scale deployment of its cement-free pavers anywhere in the world. However, CarbiCrete did not disclose the contract value, the names of the three products or the expected carbon savings.
CarbiCrete’s paving is one of several sustainability features at the delivery station. The site is also Amazon’s first building to pursue Living Future’s Zero Carbon Certification v1.1, a standard covering construction and operations. “Seeing CarbiCrete products deployed at this scale is an important milestone for our technology and for lower-carbon construction more broadly,” said Gary Belisle, CEO of CarbiCrete. “Projects like these are essential to demonstrating the potential of cement-free concrete as a lower-carbon alternative in large-scale construction,” he added.
Quick anonymous worklife pollWhat's my daily work emissions burn, or savings?Powered by ESG News
CarbiCrete’s technology replaces 100% of the cement in masonry and hardscape products with a steel-making by-product. According to the company, producing cement, the binder in conventional concrete, accounts for about 8% of global carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions. It generates over 900kg of CO2 for every 1,000kg of material produced. CarbiCrete then cures the concrete with CO2, permanently storing captured carbon and cutting projects’ embodied carbon, or materials-related emissions.
Why It Matters
For CarbiCrete, the Stockton-on-Tees site is its first wide-scale paver deployment and gives it Amazon as a named reference customer. For Amazon, the paving adds a lower-carbon material to its first building pursuing Zero Carbon Certification v1.1. CarbiCrete is also exploring how its manufacturing footprint across Canada, Europe, the U.S. and Australia could support future projects, including with Amazon. If that footprint can serve Amazon’s sites, the deployment could open a path to repeat paving and masonry orders from Amazon.
